notes.meaning: The people urge one another to turn back to God after suffering under His discipline. They recognise that the Lord Himself allowed them to be broken, yet they trust that the same God who struck them is ready to bind up their wounds. Repentance—turning away from sin and returning to the Lord—is their only true source of healing.

God promises that their ruin will not last forever, but that He will bring a speedy rescue, like raising someone from death. In Hebrew idiom, after two days and on the third day simply meant a very short time before God restored life and fellowship. Christian interpreters also see here a clear pointer to Jesus Christ rising from the dead on the third day to give life to His people.

differ.view: Martin Luther and traditional Lutheran interpreters read this verse as speaking solely of the physical resurrection of Jesus Christ on the third day.

John Calvin and many Reformed interpreters understand the verse primarily as God's promise to revive His afflicted people quickly, seeing Christ's resurrection as the true pattern and pledge of that renewal.

notes.meaning: Those who return to God are encouraged to eagerly pursue an intimate relationship with Him. The Lord's arrival to comfort and restore His people is as dependable as the morning dawn and as refreshing as spring rains on dry soil.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: A charismatic movement known as the Latter Rain Movement used this verse to teach that God would pour out a final, supernatural outpouring of spiritual power before Christ returns, restoring apostles and prophets to the church.

notes.meaning: The Lord expresses His deep sorrow over how shallow and short-lived the people's devotion really was. The loyalty of both Ephraim (the northern kingdom) and Judah disappeared as fast as early morning mist or dew under the blazing sun. Their brief moments of sorrow did not produce genuine, lasting obedience.

Because the people's repentance was so fleeting, God sent His prophets to deliver sharp and cutting warnings. The messages spoken through the prophets announced certain doom against stubborn sin, striking like a deadly sword. God's righteous judgments would go forth clearly, like blazing light for everyone to see.

The Lord explains what He truly values in His people: steadfast love, compassion, and a genuine personal knowledge of Him. In the original language, wanting mercy not sacrifice means wanting mercy rather than sacrifice. Rituals and offerings commanded in the law were empty in God's sight whenever people lacked love and obedience in their hearts.

The people broke the covenant—God's sacred, binding agreement with them—just as Adam broke God's command in the Garden of Eden. Even in the fertile land God gave them, they proved unfaithful and turned away from His ways.

differ.view: Many Reformed teachers see this verse as a direct scriptural reference to the covenant of works, in which Adam represented humanity and failed to obey God in Eden.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate the phrase as at Adam, identifying it as a specific town along the Jordan River where Israel committed an act of rebellion.

notes.meaning: Gilead, a region containing cities of refuge meant to provide safety for those fleeing accidental death, had turned into a center of criminal violence. Instead of offering justice and peace, the city was marked everywhere by the bloody tracks of murder.

The religious leaders of the land were acting like gangs of highway robbers lying in wait for victims. Priests banded together to murder and rob travelers on the road to Shechem, which was another city set apart for refuge and worship. Their sacred calling was replaced by cruel, organized crime.

The Lord looks upon Israel and sees shocking wickedness that fills Him with detestation. The northern tribes, led by Ephraim, indulged in spiritual prostitution—a term the prophets often used for worshipping idols instead of the true God. This unfaithfulness thoroughly defiled the nation.

The southern kingdom of Judah is warned that its own day of reckoning is coming because it joined in Israel's sins. Just as a farmer reaps what is planted, Judah would reap a harvest of judgment and go into exile. Even so, the verse closes with hope, pointing to a future time when God will bring His people back home.
